title: My Opening Remarks at the WSDA China National Debate Tournament
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: In a banquet speech to the WSDA China National Debate Tournament, veteran debate coach Stefan Bauschard reflects on fifteen years of building competitive speech and debate programs in China, using his own aging alongside a much younger coaching staff as a frame for a broader argument about what debate teaches in an AI era. He describes debate topics that have shifted from a one-child-policy China to today's students arguing about childcare subsidies, cashless societies, and whether people want to become cyborgs -- evidence, he says, that for this generation AI is simply "part of life" rather than a source of adult-style anxiety, something students use as a tool to sharpen arguments and research rather than fear. Bauschard reframes the founding question of his China debate work -- how to bring debate to the country -- into a new one: what education even is when a machine can do the homework, arguing there are no "AI-proof jobs" but that speech and debate specifically build the human skills of articulation, collaborative reasoning, and creative argument that he believes will define value in a post-AI world. He closes on the durability of human relationships across fifteen years of coaching, describing the renewable energy he draws from successive cohorts of students as his real reason for continuing to coach rather than retire.
points: Bauschard frames the shift in his students' own debate topics -- from a one-child-policy era to today's arguments about childcare subsidies, cashless societies, and cyborg futures -- as evidence that AI functions for this generation as an ordinary tool rather than a source of adult-style anxiety.

His central educational claim is that fifteen years after answering "how do we bring debate to China," the live question has become "what education even is when the machine can do the homework," and that there are no "AI-proof jobs," only students better or worse prepared to build in an unpredictable world.

He argues speech and debate specifically cultivate the skills he expects to matter most going forward -- articulating a position, working with others, and generating creative arguments -- because human interaction of that kind "cannot be overtaken by a machine."

The speech's emotional throughline is that human relationships, not technology or institutional achievement, are what has stayed constant across fifteen years of coaching, and that the renewable energy of successive student cohorts is the actual reason he keeps returning rather than retiring.
quotes: Right now, the debate topic for high school and middle school is basically how to encourage people to have more children: childcare subsidies versus free childcare centers. And when I first came to China, there was still a one-child policy. So that's shifted completely.

For adults, AI can be scary. Everyone can be apprehensive about what the future will bring. But these kids just take AI and use it to become wizards - to help improve their arguments, their research, their ideas. They embrace it as another tool, another relationship.
The question now is what education even is when the machine can do the homework. And everybody in this room is going to help answer that one.

We have to admit that we really have no idea exactly what students need to know to succeed in this new world. There are no AI-proof jobs. But what we can do is help students become Trailblazers - students who can build a new world and thrive in any world that gets created.

To articulate their point. To work with others. To come up with creative ideas and creative arguments. I really think these are the skills that are going to define the future. How we interact with each other as humans cannot be overtaken by a machine, and this will be essential.
But the truth is I have more energy now than I've ever had. And it isn't mine - I stole it. From these students. Their energy is renewable. It keeps going.
